Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette: John, a 45-year-old European-American male and journalist, had experienced a traumatic period of captivity that left indelible marks on his mind and body. His experience began when he was abducted while covering a conflict zone overseas. Held in a small, dark room for weeks, John was subjected to harsh conditions, including physical pain and sensory deprivation. The memory of the confinement lingers with him, manifesting through specific triggers that disrupt his daily life. One of John's most debilitating triggers is the recurring neck pain he experiences. This somatic pain serves as a constant reminder of the physical strain and discomfort he endured during captivity. Any slight touch also provokes an intense reaction; the sensation feels intrusive and invasive, reminiscent of the unwelcome hands that had controlled him in captivity. The smell of alcohol acts as another potent trigger for John. In his confined space, he was occasionally exposed to the stench of alcohol, which became associated with the dehumanizing conditions of his captors' carelessness. Now, even a whiff of alcohol can evoke a vivid replay of those distressing memories. John’s hypervigilance has become a defining feature of his daily existence. He is perpetually on edge, constantly scanning his surroundings for any signs of danger. Unexpected or loud sounds, in particular, send him into a state of alarm. His heightened senses have led to frequent false alarms; he often reacts as if he were still in peril, even when the situation is harmless. This hyperawareness has made it difficult for John to relax and enjoy his surroundings. The memories of captivity replay like a relentless film in John’s mind. He finds himself reliving those terrifying moments over and over again, with vivid detail and intense emotion. These uncontrolled intrusions are particularly distressing, as they force their way into his consciousness at times when he does not want to be reminded of the trauma. For example, while working late one night in his office, John was suddenly hit by a wave of nausea and sweating upon hearing a loud noise outside. His mind immediately flashed back to the sound of guards’ footsteps echoing through the concrete walls of his cell. He felt an overwhelming sense of terror, as if he were once again trapped and powerless. Similarly, during a recent dinner with his wife at a restaurant where wine was being served, John’s heart raced upon catching the smell of alcohol. The memory of his captivity surged back, causing him to leave abruptly in an attempt to escape the triggering environment. This incident left both John and his wife deeply troubled, as it underscored how the trauma had affected their relationship. Over time, these triggers have led to significant avoidance behaviors. John has become reluctant to participate in social gatherings where alcohol is present or situations that might involve physical contact. His hypervigilance has also made it difficult for him to concentrate on his work, leading to a noticeable decline in his productivity and engagement as a journalist. What frightens John most is the prospect of never regaining a sense of normalcy in his life. The constant intrusions of memory and heightened threat responses have left him feeling isolated and overwhelmed. His wife has noticed that he has become distant and withdrawn, and this has put strain on their relationship. It was one particularly harrowing incident at work that finally pushed John to seek help. He had a panic attack during an interview, unable to concentrate due to the constant ringing in his ears—a sound reminiscent of the chains clanking in his cell. His wife, deeply concerned about his well-being and the impact on their lives, encouraged him to see a therapist. In therapy sessions, John hopes to regain control over his life and find ways to manage his triggers without avoiding important aspects of his daily routine. He is most hopeful for a future where he can navigate his environment with less fear and more peace, allowing him to reconnect with his family and return to the work he loves without the constant shadow of trauma hanging over him.
